title: Stories of a Great Journey
objective: Students will learn that the Harlem Renaissance grew from the Great Migration — a great journey of Black families moving north — and that the people who made that journey created music, stories, and art that changed America. They will connect this to their own experiences of change and discover that ordinary people can do extraordinary things.
materials: Device to play a short audio clip of Bessie Smith or Louis Armstrong (freely available on YouTube or Smithsonian Folkways)
Simple projected or printed US map showing Southern states and New York
Differentiated student handouts (Green / Yellow / Red) — print one per student before class
Crayons or colored pencils for drawing activities
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the exhibition:** If the Harlem Renaissance exhibition is available at your school, bring your class to experience the phonograph, the Great Migration Map, the Jazz Lab, and more firsthand. Ask your librarian to arrange a visit.
**Option 2 — Virtual visit:** Explore the full exhibition online.

steps.title: A song from far away
script: Play 60 seconds of Bessie Smith or a Harlem-era jazz recording. Let students simply listen with eyes closed.
*“Close your eyes and just listen. What do you feel? What pictures do you see in your mind?”*
Take two or three responses, then:

*“This music is almost 100 years old! It was made by people who had just finished one of the longest, bravest journeys in American history. Today we are going to find out who they were — and what they made.”*

screen.question: Close your eyes and just listen. What do you feel? What pictures do you see in your mind?

steps.purpose: Listen before learning anything: let the music raise the questions.

steps.title: The big move
script: Show the US map. Point to the Deep South, then trace a path north to New York.

*“A long time ago, many Black families lived in the South of America — places like Mississippi and Georgia. Life was very hard and unfair there. So families packed everything they owned and moved north — to cities like Chicago and New York. We call this the Great Migration. When they arrived in a neighborhood called Harlem, something amazing happened: musicians, writers, poets, and painters all found each other. They started making something the world had never seen before — a Renaissance. That means a great burst of new ideas and beauty.”*

steps.purpose: Trace the Great Migration from the South to Harlem.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Distribute differentiated handouts. Let students self-select their level, or assign based on your knowledge of their needs.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Students draw their family’s journey on a map outline, label where they came from and where they live now, and draw one thing their family brought with them. Sentence frames support emerging writers.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Students write about a personal experience of change, connect it to the Great Migration, and write about what they would create if they lived in Harlem in 1925.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Students write a first-person “interview” with an imaginary Great Migration traveler, then independently research one real Harlem Renaissance figure and write three facts. Suggest: Langston Hughes, Bessie Smith, Duke Ellington, Zora Neale Hurston, Aaron Douglas, or Walter F. White.

steps.purpose: Connect the great journey to each child’s own story of change.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. You can switch at any time.

steps.title: What they carried
script: *“The people who made the Great Migration left behind their homes and sometimes their families. But they brought their music, their stories, their faith, and their creativity. And in Harlem, they used all of that to make something so beautiful it still lives today — in every jazz song, every poem, every painting.”*

screen.text: But they brought their music, their stories, their faith, and their creativity.

steps.purpose: Close on what the travelers carried with them, and what it became.
students: What would you bring with you?
